column3: The structures P and Q are shown. Unknown samples X and Y correspond to these two isomers. An OH···O interaction in X persists after large dilution in an inert solvent; Y instead loses intermolecular association on dilution. Masking the OH donor by O-methylation removes those respective interactions. Both original vapours contain molecules of molar mass 139 g mol−1, and X is more readily steam-distilled. Which combined interpretation fits the geometry and controls?
column4: X is Q and Y is P; persistence on dilution proves an intermolecular network
column5: X is P and Y is Q; equal vapour molar masses require equal liquid intermolecular forces
column6: X is P and Y is Q; internal hydrogen bonding can persist on dilution while a less interconnected liquid is more volatile
column7: X is P and Y is Q; masking OH proves that hydrogen bonding permanently changes the covalent molecular formula
column9:
Answer: (C) X matches the ortho geometry P and Y the para geometry Q; the controls distinguish internal from intermolecular hydrogen bonding.
Step 1: Adjacent OH and nitro oxygen in P permit an internal donor–acceptor contact. Opposite positions in Q do not provide the corresponding short internal contact.
Step 2: Dilution separates molecules and disrupts intermolecular association without necessarily breaking a within-molecule interaction. The masking control removes the OH donor, supporting the specific role of that group rather than a general mass effect.
Step 3: Reduced intermolecular networking helps explain X being more volatile; equal monomer masses in vapour do not make the liquid interactions equal.
Why: Geometry, concentration dependence and removal of a donor are independent constraints. No dimer fraction or covalent polymerisation follows from these qualitative controls.
Why not the others: (A) reverses the positional assignment and the concentration argument. (B) confuses equal molecular mass with equal liquid association. (D) mistakes reversible noncovalent interaction for a changed molecular formula.
Key point: Test an interaction through geometry and controlled perturbation, not molar mass alone.
column10: Geometrical, dilution and donor-masking controls distinguish internal hydrogen bonding from a liquid network

column3: In a metal carbonyl, CO donates electron density from a filled orbital toward the metal, while the metal can return density from filled d orbitals into a CO antibonding orbital. Which joint bond trend is expected when the second interaction is strengthened within this model?
column4: Metal–carbon bonding strengthens while the internal carbon–oxygen bond weakens
column5: Both bonds necessarily weaken because every donation removes a bonding pair
column6: The C–O bond strengthens because its antibonding occupancy rises
column7: No interaction is possible because CO has no donor electron pair
column9:
Answer: (A) Stronger back-donation reinforces metal–carbon bonding and weakens the internal CO bond.
Why: The two interactions are complementary: sigma donation from CO helps establish the metal–ligand connection, and metal-to-ligand pi back-donation adds another bonding contribution between those partners. The receiving CO orbital is antibonding with respect to its own C–O bond, so increasing occupancy there lowers the internal bond order. Metal–ligand strength and intraligand strength can therefore change in opposite directions.
Why not the others: (B) ignores the bonding role of the metal–ligand overlap. (C) reverses the consequence of occupying an antibonding orbital. (D) denies the donor interaction specified in the question and present in the carbonyl model.
Key point: Identify which bond an orbital is bonding or antibonding with respect to.
column10: Synergic carbonyl donation strengthens one bond while weakening another
column11: Coordination Compounds: bonding in metal carbonyls

column3: An insulated vessel has heat capacity 50 J K−1 and contains 10.0 g ice at 0 degrees C. It receives 4000 J. Use latent heat of fusion 334 J g−1 and liquid-water specific heat 4.20 J g−1 K−1, and neglect all other heat capacities and losses. Which final state follows?
column4: Some ice remains at 0 degrees C
column5: All ice melts; temperature is 4000/92 degrees C
column6: All ice melts; temperature is 660/42 degrees C
column7: All ice melts; temperature is 660/92 degrees C
column9:
Answer: (D) All ice melts and the final temperature is 660/92≈7.17 degrees C.
Given: The ice and vessel start at the melting temperature.
Formula/Principle: Supply latent heat before sensible heating, including the vessel only when temperature rises.
Step 1: Complete melting requires \[Q_{fus}=10.0(334)=3340\ \mathrm J.\] The 4000 J input exceeds this.
Step 2: The remaining 660 J warms water and vessel together, whose combined heat capacity is \[C=10.0(4.20)+50=92\ \mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}.\]
Step 3: \[T_f=0+660/92\approx7.17\ ^\circ\mathrm C.\]
Why: The energy budget crosses a phase boundary; neither one heat-capacity division nor latent heat alone describes the complete process.
Why not the others: (A) ignores that input exceeds complete fusion heat. (B) omits latent heat. (C) omits vessel heating after melting.
Key point: Account for every phase and every body whose temperature changes.
column10: Fusion threshold followed by shared water-and-vessel sensible heating
column11: Thermodynamics: calorimetry; enthalpy of phase change

column3: A molecule contains a ketone and a separate cyclic acetal. The ketone must become a methylene group while the acetal remains protected. Assume the molecule tolerates heating and that only the stated functional groups react. Which choice and explanation best meet the requirement?
column4: Zn(Hg)/concentrated HCl, because acetals require base for hydrolysis
column5: Hydrazine followed by KOH and heat, because Wolff–Kishner reduction removes the ketone oxygen under basic conditions while the acetal resists base
column6: NaBH4 followed by aqueous acid, because NaBH4 directly replaces C=O by CH2
column7: Aqueous acid alone, because acetal hydrolysis also reduces the ketone
column9:
Answer: (B) Wolff–Kishner conditions reduce the ketone while preserving the base-stable acetal.
Why: The ketone first condenses with hydrazine to form a hydrazone. Strong base and heat then convert that group into a methylene group with loss of nitrogen. The separate acetal is stable to these basic conditions; it is normally hydrolysed back to a carbonyl compound in aqueous acid. Thus the choice must satisfy both the desired reduction and the survival of the protecting group. Clemmensen reduction can remove a ketone oxygen, but its strongly acidic aqueous medium threatens the acetal, so choosing a reduction name alone is insufficient.
Why not the others: (A) reverses acetal stability: Zn(Hg)/HCl is acidic and can deprotect it. (C) NaBH4 gives an alcohol rather than a methylene group, and the later acid also threatens the acetal. (D) Acid hydrolyses an acetal but supplies no ketone-to-methylene reduction.
Key point: Select reaction conditions using both the target transformation and the stability of every retained functional group.
column10: Reduction conditions must remove a ketone oxygen while preserving an acid-sensitive acetal
column11: Aldehydes and Ketones: chemical reactions; reduction to hydrocarbons; acetal formation and hydrolysis

column3: Equal iron surfaces are coated with zinc or copper and then scratched to expose iron while coating and iron remain electrically connected in moist electrolyte. Standard reduction potentials are Zn2+/Zn=-0.76 V, Fe2+/Fe=-0.44 V and Cu2+/Cu=+0.34 V. Which comparison follows from galvanic action at the scratches?
column4: Both coatings protect equally because neither scratch changes the coating metal's identity
column5: Copper sacrifices itself preferentially, whereas zinc makes iron the anode
column6: Zinc can remain sacrificial to iron; copper can instead make exposed iron the anodic partner
column7: Iron must remain cathodic against both metals because it is beneath a coating
column9:
Answer: (C) Zinc can protect sacrificially, whereas copper can promote anodic iron dissolution at a scratch.
Step 1: Zinc's more negative reduction potential makes its oxidation favourable relative to iron in this comparison. Connected zinc can supply electrons while iron acts as the protected cathodic partner.
Step 2: Copper is more noble than iron. Exposed iron coupled to copper can instead become the anode and dissolve.
Why: An intact barrier and a galvanically connected scratched coating are different protection situations. The potential order determines which metal sacrifices itself; the mere presence of a metallic layer does not fix that order.
Why not the others: (A) ignores the exposed galvanic junction. (B) reverses the supplied potential order. (D) infers electrode role from geometrical position instead of electrochemical tendency.
Key point: Reassess coating protection after the substrate becomes exposed.
column10: Scratches separate sacrificial-zinc protection from a noble-metal galvanic coating

column3: An amide CH3–13CO–NH2 has only its carbonyl carbon labelled 13C. Route P treats it with Br2/aqueous NaOH, isolates the resulting primary amine, then applies ordinary nitrous-acid deamination. Route Q instead reduces the amide with LiAlH4, isolates the primary amine, and applies the same deamination. No carbon scrambling occurs. Which final alcohols and label locations are expected?
column4: P gives labelled ethanol; Q gives unlabelled methanol
column5: P gives unlabelled methanol; Q gives ethanol labelled at its OH-bearing carbon
column6: Both give ethanol labelled at its methyl carbon
column7: Both give unlabelled methanol because every amide reduction removes its carbonyl carbon
column9:
Answer: (B) P gives unlabelled methanol and Q gives ethanol with 13C at the OH-bearing carbon.
Step 1: Hofmann bromamide degradation removes the amide carbonyl carbon from the organic amine. P therefore gives CH3NH2, with the label excluded from that one-carbon product.
Step 2: Ordinary aliphatic primary-amine deamination replaces NH2 by OH with nitrogen evolution, giving unlabelled CH3OH.
Step 3: Hydride reduction retains the amide carbonyl carbon as the amine-bearing methylene, giving CH3–13CH2–NH2 in Q. Deamination then gives CH3–13CH2–OH.
Why: The two amide-to-amine methods have different carbon-retention rules; the common later step preserves that difference. Tracking the labelled atom through each reaction is necessary, not just counting the original total carbons.
Why not the others: (A) exchanges the two preparation methods. (C) retains a carbon lost in P and moves the Q label to the wrong carbon. (D) incorrectly applies Hofmann carbon loss to hydride reduction.
Key point: Track the amide carbonyl carbon before applying a later common reaction.
column10: Two amide-to-amine routes retain different labelled carbons before a common deamination
column11: Amines: preparation by amide reduction and Hofmann bromamide reaction; reactions with nitrous acid

column3: A 2.32 g sample of pure Fe3O4 is dissolved in acid without changing its iron oxidation states. The Fe2+ present is then titrated completely with 0.0200 M acidified KMnO4; Fe3+ does not react further. Use molar mass Fe3O4=232 g mol−1. What titrant volume is required, and how many moles of Fe3+ are present after titration?
column9:
Answer: (B) The volume is 100 mL and final Fe3+ amount is 0.0300 mol.
Given: Fe3O4 contains one Fe(II) and two Fe(III) centres per formula unit.
Formula/Principle: Only the Fe(II) fraction supplies electrons; one acidified permanganate ion accepts five electrons.
Step 1: \[n_{oxide}=2.32/232=0.0100\ \mathrm{mol},\quad n_{Fe^{2+}}=0.0100\ \mathrm{mol}.\]
Step 2: \[\ce{MnO4-}+5\ce{Fe^{2+}}+8\ce{H+}\longrightarrow\ce{Mn^{2+}}+5\ce{Fe^{3+}}+4\ce{H2O}.\] Thus titrant moles are 0.0100/5=0.00200.
Step 3: \[V=0.00200/0.0200=0.100\ \mathrm L;\qquad n_{Fe^{3+},final}=0.0200+0.0100=0.0300\ \mathrm{mol}.\]
Why: The average iron oxidation number is not a population of identical iron ions for the selective redox assay.
Why not the others: (A) treats all iron as Fe(II). (C) omits initially present Fe(III). (D) divides the volume by five a second time.
Key point: Resolve mixed valence before counting titratable electrons.
column10: Mixed-valence iron accounting precedes selective permanganate demand
column11: Redox Reactions: oxidation number; electron balance; The d-Block Elements

column3: At constant volume the reaction is 2A→3B. Over 30.0 s, [A] falls from 0.200 to 0.140 M, and no other reaction occurs. Using the stoichiometrically normalised average reaction rate, what are that rate and the increase in [B]?
column9:
Answer: (D) Average reaction rate is 0.00100 M s⁻¹ and B rises by 0.0900 M.
Given: A decreases by 0.0600 M in 30.0 s and the reaction coefficients are 2 and 3.
Formula/Principle: \(r_{avg}=- rac12\Delta[A]/\Delta t= rac13\Delta[B]/\Delta t\).
Step 1: A disappearance rate is 0.0600/30.0=0.00200 M s⁻¹, so \[r_{avg}=0.00200/2=0.00100\ \mathrm{M\,s^{-1}}.\]
Step 2: The stoichiometric extent in concentration units is 0.0600/2=0.0300 M, giving \[\Delta[B]=3(0.0300)=0.0900\ \mathrm M.\]
Why: Different species have different appearance or disappearance rates, while division by their stoichiometric coefficients defines one common reaction rate. One interval does not determine reaction order.
Why not the others: (A) reports A disappearance instead of the normalised rate. (B) assumes a 1:1 A-to-B conversion. (C) makes both errors.
Key point: Normalise the rate and conserve stoichiometric amounts separately.
column10: Species disappearance rate differs from the normalised reaction rate and product concentration rise
column11: Chemical Kinetics: rate of a reaction; stoichiometric rate definition

column3: For chlorobutanoic-acid isomers, the chlorine atom is placed at C2, C3 or C4, counting the carboxyl carbon as C1. Only the distance of this identical substituent from COOH changes. Which expected acidity order and conjugate-base order follow from the inductive effect?
column6: All acidities identical because the molecular formula is unchanged
column9:
Answer: (A) The nearer electron-withdrawing chlorine enhances acidity more, reversing the conjugate-base basicity order.
Why: Chlorine withdraws electron density through sigma bonds. Its stabilising influence on a nearby carboxylate is strongest when closest to the acid group and decreases with distance along the chain. More stable carboxylate corresponds to easier acid dissociation, so the C2-substituted acid is strongest in this comparison. The conjugate base of a stronger acid is correspondingly weaker under the same conditions. Positional isomers need not have identical acidity even though their elemental formulas agree.
Why not the others: (B) reverses the distance dependence for acidity. (C) treats composition as a complete description of electronic effects. (D) makes conjugate-base basicity increase with its parent acid's acidity.
Key point: Compare both substituent distance and the direction of the conjugate-acid/base relation.
column10: Distance-dependent induction reverses the corresponding carboxylate basicity order
column11: Aldehydes, Ketones and Carboxylic Acids: acidity; inductive effect

column3: The structure in the figure is HOCH2–CH=CH–COOH, with the higher-priority groups CH2OH and COOH on opposite sides of the double bond. Which name respects the principal functional group, numbering and alkene configuration?
column9:
Answer: (C) (E)-4-Hydroxybut-2-enoic acid.
Step 1: Carboxylic acid is the principal functional group, so its carbon is C1 and the four-carbon parent is butenoic acid. The double bond lies between C2 and C3; the OH-bearing terminal carbon is C4.
Step 2: On each alkene carbon the carbon-containing group has priority over hydrogen. The given opposite placement is E.
Why: Functional-group priority determines the parent and numbering before the stereodescriptor is assigned. Merely numbering from the alcohol end would give a plausible-looking but inconsistent name.
Why not the others: (A) assigns the opposite alkene configuration. (B) puts the hydroxyl on the acid carbon rather than on the terminal CH2 group. (D) makes the alcohol the principal suffix and changes the parent description.
Key point: Determine principal group, locants and configuration in that order.

column11: Organic Chemistry—Basic Principles: nomenclature; geometrical isomerism

column3: A sealed dilute solution contains 10.0 g of a molecular solute per litre and has osmotic pressure π=0.100 RT in consistent litre–mole units. Its membrane passes only solvent. The solute is volatile and contributes to the total equilibrium vapour pressure. Which inference is justified?
column4: Osmotic molar mass is 100 g mol−1; the simple nonvolatile-solute vapour-pressure-lowering formula cannot be used on total pressure
column5: Osmotic molar mass is negative because total vapour pressure can exceed the pure solvent pressure
column6: Volatility alone makes the retained-solute osmotic measurement impossible
column7: Both measurements must give 10.0 g mol−1 without accounting for solute vapour
column9:
Answer: (A) The osmotic result is usable under the stated membrane condition; total vapour pressure requires both components.
Given: The vessel is sealed and the membrane excludes the solute, preventing loss or leakage from invalidating the stated concentration.
Formula/Principle: \(\pi=cRT\) for the dilute molecular solution, while volatile-component total pressure is the sum of both partial pressures.
Step 1: \[c=\pi/(RT)=0.100\ \mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}}.\]
Step 2: \[M= rac{10.0\ \mathrm{g\,L^{-1}}}{0.100\ \mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}}}=100\ \mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}.\]
Why: The nonvolatile-solute lowering formula assumes the solute does not itself supply vapour pressure. That assumption is distinct from solute exclusion by an osmotic membrane.
Why not the others: (B) converts failure of an inappropriate vapour formula into an impossible mass. (C) ignores the explicit retention and sealed-system assumptions. (D) neither follows the osmotic division nor includes solute vapour.
Key point: Check the separate physical assumptions of two colligative measurements.
column10: Volatility invalidates a simplified total-vapour inference but not a sealed retained-solute osmotic measurement
column11: Solutions: vapour pressure; osmotic pressure; molar-mass determination

column3: Complete combustion of 0.800 g of a compound containing only carbon and hydrogen gives 0.0500 mol CO2 and 0.100 mol H2O. The oxidant feed contains 0.150 mol total gas, 80.0 percent O2 and 20.0 percent inert gas; all carbon and hydrogen reach the stated products. What are the empirical formula and residual O2 amount? Use C=12,H=1.
column9:
Answer: (C) CH4 and 0.0200 mol oxygen remaining.
Given: The oxidant's stated total includes inert gas.
Formula/Principle: Product atom balances determine empirical composition and actual oxygen consumption.
Step 1: Carbon is 0.0500 mol and hydrogen atoms are 2(0.100)=0.200 mol, giving C:H=1:4. Their masses sum to \(0.0500(12)+0.200(1)=0.800\) g, checking the sample.
Step 2: Product oxygen demand is \[n_{O_2}=n_{CO_2}+	frac12n_{H_2O}=0.0500+0.0500=0.100\ \mathrm{mol}.\]
Step 3: Available oxygen is \(0.150(0.800)=0.120\) mol, leaving \[0.120-0.100=0.0200\ \mathrm{mol}.\]
Why: Oxygen is in excess and the organic sample is completely consumed. Counting inert feed as oxygen would overstate the excess.
Why not the others: (A) forgets the two hydrogen atoms per water molecule. (B) treats the entire feed as oxygen. (D) does not reduce the empirical ratio and ignores oxygen consumption.
Key point: Separate feed composition from reaction stoichiometry.
column10: Impure oxidant and combustion products jointly fix empirical ratio and excess oxygen
column11: Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry: empirical formula; combustion; limiting reagents

column3: Argon has atomic number 18 and relative atomic mass about 39.95; potassium has atomic number 19 and mass about 39.10. Which placement is consistent with the modern periodic law?
column4: Potassium precedes argon because its relative atomic mass is lower
column5: Argon precedes potassium because atomic number, not atomic mass, defines the modern ordering
column6: They occupy one position because both masses are close to 40
column7: Their order depends on how many neutrons a particular isotope contains
column9:
Answer: (B) Atomic numbers 18 then 19 fix argon before potassium.
Why: The modern periodic law relates periodic properties to atomic number. Relative atomic mass is an abundance-weighted isotopic property and need not increase in the same order for every adjacent pair. Argon–potassium illustrates why a mass-only ordering cannot replace the nuclear-charge ordering. Isotopes of the same element retain its atomic number and therefore do not receive separate periodic-table positions.
Why not the others: (A) reapplies an atomic-mass criterion instead of the modern law. (C) treats approximate mass equality as equality of element identity. (D) uses neutron count where nuclear charge is required.
Key point: Keep elemental ordering distinct from isotopic mass.
column10: The argon–potassium mass inversion tests the actual variable in the modern periodic law
column11: Classification of Elements: modern periodic law; atomic number

column3: A model compares prolonged impairment of fat absorption with a short period of low vitamin-C intake. Which statement best uses vitamin solubility without claiming that every water-soluble vitamin has identical storage behaviour?
column4: All vitamins are stored equally, so solubility cannot affect deficiency risk
column5: Vitamin C must require fat absorption because its name includes a letter
column6: Fat malabsorption selectively prevents absorption of B vitamins but leaves A,D,E,K unaffected
column7: Fat-soluble A,D,E,K are particularly vulnerable to impaired fat absorption; vitamin-C intake and limited reserves can produce a different time course
column9:
Answer: (D) Solubility influences absorption and storage, but does not impose one universal deficiency timetable.
Why: Vitamins A,D,E and K are fat soluble and can be affected when fat absorption is impaired. Vitamin C is water soluble and is not stored in the same way as typical fat-soluble reserves, so inadequate intake may produce a different time course. Water solubility must not be turned into an exceptionless statement that every B vitamin has no significant stores; vitamin B12 is an important storage exception. The question concerns the supported class distinction rather than diagnosing a specific patient from duration alone.
Why not the others: (A) removes meaningful absorption and storage differences. (B) classifies chemistry from a name. (C) reverses the solubility-related absorption vulnerability.
Key point: Use solubility as a biological constraint while retaining known exceptions.
column10: Vitamin solubility predicts absorption vulnerability without an absolute rule about all water-soluble stores
column11: Biomolecules: vitamins; water- and fat-soluble groups

column3: A 0.100 M salt BH+A− is formed from weak base B with Kb=10−6 and weak acid HA with Ka=10−4. At 25 degrees C take Kw=10−14 and use the usual weak-acid/weak-base salt hydrolysis approximation. What pH and interpretation follow?
column4: Approximately 6; BH+ acidity exceeds the basic influence of A−
column5: Exactly 7; every 1:1 salt must be neutral
column6: Approximately 8; the weaker parent base makes its conjugate acid weaker
column7: Approximately 4; the salt behaves as 0.100 M strong acid
column9:
Answer: (A) The salt is acidic, with approximate pH 6.
Given: Parent-base Kb=10⁻⁶ and parent-acid Ka=10⁻⁴.
Formula/Principle: Both ions hydrolyse; \(pH=7+	frac12\log(K_b/K_a)\) under the specified approximation.
Step 1: Their separate constants are \[K_a(BH^+)=K_w/K_b=10^{-8},\quad K_b(A^-)=K_w/K_a=10^{-10}.\] The cation's acidic action is stronger.
Step 2: \[pH=7+	frac12\log(10^{-6}/10^{-4})=7-1=6.\]
Why: Equal stoichiometric charges do not mean equal acid and base strengths. Both parent equilibria, not only the 1:1 salt formula, determine hydrolysis.
Why not the others: (B) confuses electrical neutrality with neutral pH. (C) reverses the conjugate-strength relation and the logarithmic ratio. (D) treats weak hydrolysis as complete strong-acid dissociation.
Key point: Recover both conjugate-ion constants before interpreting a weak/weak salt.
column10: Both conjugate-ion hydrolyses determine the pH of a weak-acid weak-base salt
column11: Equilibrium: ionic equilibrium; hydrolysis of salts
